To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
morph differences in buttonwood (Cononocarpus erects) affect herbivory, and that these differences are modified by storm disturbance.

(1) green buttonwood shrubs are more nutritious to herbivores than silver shrubs, but silver shrubs are better defended; (2) storm damage increases herbivory on silver shrubs, whereas it has little effect on herbivory on green shrubs; and (3) the effects of storm damage on herbivory are mediated by morphological changes in shrubs.

(i) green morph buttonwood shrubs produce tougher, but less nutritious, leaves than silver morph shrubs; (ii) green morph leaves are less damaged by herbivores; (iii) silver morph shrubs have higher levels of herbivore damage than green morph shrubs; and (iv) disturbance, particularly simulated hurricane surge, can modify morph differences in buttonwood.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the consequences of disturbance on the interactions of plants with their herbivores.
understanding how morphological variation in plants influences herbivore resistance and how disturbance influences the relative importance of different plant traits for herbivory.
the consequences of disturbance for plant-herbivore interactions and with the consequences of morphological variation in plants for these interactions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
disturbance can have a significant impact on herbivory and morphological characteristics of the polymorphic buttonwood shrub.
morph differences in buttonwood are important for herbivores.
morphs of buttonwood have strong effects on herbivores, which are in turn affected by disturbance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the green morph is more resistant to herbivores, but the silver morph is more resistant in the presence of damage.
silver morphs of buttonwood are more susceptible to herbivores than green morphs, but that this difference is diminished by disturbance.
disturbance has strong consequences for the herbivory of buttonwood and these effects vary between morphs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the morphological and physiological characteristics of plants that make them resistant to one type of damage may make them more susceptible to other types.
morphological and chemical differences between green and silver buttonwood shrubs have important consequences for the resistance of these shrubs to herbivores.
disturbance can alter the balance of resistance traits in a way that favors herbivores, with implications for plant defense theory and the role of disturbance in community ecology.
